_about: Student-facing content for each quarter. One source: screens read only from here. Wording follows section 1A of the design (plain, conversational). {placeholders} are filled from the team's results.

briefing.headline: Your first quarter: find out what actually makes money
paragraphs: The old presidents' settings are still running. Fourteen drilling rigs are working in Texas, Baton Rouge is running at 96%, and Rotterdam is running at 82% after losing money in three of the last four quarters.
Marcus Delacroix thinks Rotterdam should be sold. Ingrid Vestergaard thinks Texas could drill more. Neither of them has shown you numbers that compare one part of Halden with another.
Oil prices slipped over the holidays. Grant Whitaker wants to know by Thursday whether you'll change anything this quarter, and why.
briefing.question: Which parts of Halden really make money, and how many rigs should drill in Texas?

1.rule: A rig costs $40 million a quarter. Each extra rig drills poorer ground than the one before, so it adds less oil. New wells take about three months to start pumping. In Norway, the government takes 78% of the profit on every barrel, and it also absorbs 78% of any loss. A refinery has costs that come with each barrel it runs and costs it pays whether it runs or not.
1.new_pages_note: This quarter you can change the oil fields and the refineries. Gas station prices open next quarter.

exhibits.title: The asset register: every oil field, refinery and gas station business, with its costs
Python notebook with the same data (optional)

1.marchetti: Oil dropped from $73 to $71 a barrel over the winter. Refining margins on the Gulf Coast held up, around $22 a barrel. Europe is weak: refiners near Rotterdam are making about $4 a barrel. I wouldn't plan on prices bouncing back quickly, but I wouldn't plan on a collapse either.

bands.title: Fewer rigs, more cash
paragraphs: You cut Texas to {rigs} rigs. Drilling spending fell, and free cash flow came in at {fcf}. Ingrid asked Grant why Texas was drilling less while oil was still above $70.
Texas output was {permian_prod} barrels a day this quarter. Fewer rigs means less new oil from next quarter on, so watch how fast that number slides.

bands.title: Steady as she goes
paragraphs: You kept Texas at about the old presidents' level, {rigs} rigs. Nothing surprised anyone, including Grant.
Texas output was {permian_prod} barrels a day. Whether each of those rigs earns back its $40 million is still an open question.

bands.title: Texas drilled hard
paragraphs: You pushed Texas to {rigs} rigs. Ingrid was delighted. Grant noticed that drilling spending jumped, and free cash flow came in at {fcf}.
The new wells start pumping next quarter. Each extra rig drilled poorer ground than the last one, so the question is whether they pay for themselves.

story.closing: Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, you'll also set prices at the gas stations.

news.title: Oil drifts lower
news.body: Crude slipped to about $71 a barrel. Most producers in your class kept drilling at last year's pace.

news.title: Rotterdam's neighbours struggle
news.body: European refiners are making about $4 a barrel. Two plants near Rotterdam cut their runs over the winter.

marcus.why: You went to Baton Rouge first.

ingrid.why: You met her first and listened.
You met Ingrid before him. He noticed.

briefing.headline: Danielle wants to cut prices. Elena wants to see the numbers first.
paragraphs: A rival chain has been running ads about cheaper gas across Louisiana. Danielle Roy says Cordell is losing drivers and wants to cut what Cordell charges its station owners everywhere.

Elena Marchetti says a few cents means very different things in a city with a station on every corner and in a small town with one station for miles. She's pulled four years of prices and sales by type of market.
Most Cordell stations are owned by dealers. You set what Cordell charges them. They decide what drivers pay.
briefing.question: What should Cordell charge its station owners in each kind of market, and what should Halden charge drivers in Europe?

2.rule: When you change what Cordell charges a dealer, the dealer passes part of it on to drivers. City dealers pass on about 82 cents of every dollar; small-town dealers about 42 cents. City drivers switch stations over a few cents; small-town drivers barely notice. If you keep a price rise in place, more drivers drift away each quarter. If you cut prices, rivals start matching you, so the extra drivers fade. In Europe, Halden owns its stations and sets the pump price directly.
2.new_pages_note: New this quarter: gas station prices.

exhibits.title: Four years of prices and sales, by type of market
Python notebook with the same data (optional)

2.marchetti: Oil is flat at about $70.50. What matters this quarter is how drivers react to price. In cities they react a lot. In small towns and on highways, hardly at all. One national price would be wrong almost everywhere.

bands.title: Cheaper gas, busier stations
paragraphs: You cut prices on average. Stations got busier in the cities, and Danielle sent the whole sales team a note of congratulations.
Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}. Rival chains noticed the cuts. Expect some of them to match you next quarter.

bands.title: Prices held
paragraphs: You left prices about where they were. Danielle thinks you missed a chance. Elena thinks you didn't have to change anything to find out what drivers would do.
Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}.

bands.title: Higher prices, fewer drivers where it counts
paragraphs: You raised prices on average. Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}. In the cities, a few drivers went elsewhere. In the small towns, almost nobody noticed.
Price rises that last tend to cost more drivers over time. Keep an eye on traffic.

story.closing: Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, Rotterdam's future is on the table.

news.title: Price war talk in Louisiana
news.body: Two chains cut street prices by a few cents in Baton Rouge and New Orleans. Small-town prices barely moved.

news.title: European margins tick up
news.body: Refiners around Rotterdam made a little over $5 a barrel this quarter, the best in a year.

down.why: You took her advice on prices.

flat.why: She asked for price cuts and didn't get them.

up.why: You raised prices while she was asking for cuts.

briefing.headline: Rotterdam asks to know its future
paragraphs: The works council in Rotterdam has written to Sandvik. They want to know whether the refinery has a future before they agree to the winter maintenance plan.

Bjørn Aasen says Rotterdam covers its running costs and should keep going. Marcus says it loses money every year and should be closed or sold. Straits Pacific, meanwhile, wants to know how hard you'd like Singapore to run this quarter.
You now have more choices for Rotterdam: keep running, pause it, or close it for good.
briefing.question: Should Rotterdam keep running, slow down, pause, or close?

3.rule: Rotterdam earns the European refining margin plus $1.50 a barrel, and spends $4.10 a barrel on costs that come with each barrel it runs. It also pays $2.30 a barrel of fixed costs (staff, upkeep) on its full size whether it runs or not. Pausing stops the per-barrel costs but not the fixed ones, plus $5 million a quarter of care costs. Restarting after a pause costs $85 million. Closing costs $150 million once and is permanent. Singapore is a request: Straits Pacific owns 60% and decides.
3.new_pages_note: New this quarter: pause or close Rotterdam, and what you ask Singapore for.

exhibits.title: What each refinery spends, per barrel and fixed
What it would take to restart Rotterdam
Refining margins month by month, three regions
Who decides what at the Singapore joint venture
Worked example: a refinery deciding whether to run

3.marchetti: Oil is up a little, to about $72.60. Europe's refining margin is near $4.90 a barrel, better than last winter but still thin. If you're deciding about Rotterdam, the number to compare it with isn't whether it makes a profit. It's whether it covers the costs that stop when it stops.

bands.title: Rotterdam is closing
paragraphs: You closed Rotterdam. The one-time cost hit this quarter, and the works council has asked for a meeting with Sandvik.
Halden no longer carries Rotterdam's losses. It also no longer earns anything from Europe's refining margin, whatever happens to it from here.

bands.title: Rotterdam goes quiet
paragraphs: You paused Rotterdam. The plant stopped buying crude, but the staff, the upkeep and the care costs are still on the books: Rotterdam cost {rotterdam} this quarter.
Restarting will cost $85 million. Bjørn has asked how long you expect the pause to last.

bands.title: Rotterdam runs on
paragraphs: You kept Rotterdam running hard. It still lost money after its fixed costs ({rotterdam} this quarter), but less than it would have running slowly.
The works council has agreed to the maintenance plan. Marcus says you're throwing good money after bad. Bjørn says you're the first person in years to understand the plant.

bands.title: Rotterdam, slowed down
paragraphs: You kept Rotterdam running, but slowly. It lost {rotterdam} this quarter after its fixed costs.
Bjørn warns that equipment run slowly for a long time starts to act up. The works council is still waiting for an answer.

story.closing: Straits Pacific ran Singapore at {sg_accepted}%. Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, Geneva's results raise a question about how Halden charges itself for crude.

news.title: European refiners pick different paths
news.body: Some companies in your class slowed or paused their European refineries this quarter. Others kept running. Traders are watching what that does to Europe's refining margin.

news.title: Singapore partners stay cautious
news.body: Asian refining margins were steady at a little over $12 a barrel.

closed.why: You closed a plant he spent 20 years running.
He's wanted Rotterdam gone for years.

idle.why: He doesn't trust a pause to stay a pause.

running_hard.why: You kept the plant he wants to sell.

running_slow.why: He thinks running slowly is the worst of both.

briefing.headline: Geneva just had its best quarter in four years
paragraphs: Lorenz Kuhn's trading desk in Geneva just had its best quarter in four years. Marcus Delacroix noticed first. About half of Geneva's profit came from one trick: buying Texas crude cheaply on the open market while Baton Rouge kept paying Halden's own, higher price for it.

Marcus wants the price Baton Rouge pays to be what the crude actually costs to pump and ship. The oil fields team wants it to stay at the market price. Kuhn says he's fine either way, and that's exactly what worries Grant Whitaker, the CFO.
briefing.question: How much should Baton Rouge pay Halden's own oil fields for Texas crude?

4.rule: When Halden's own crude price is different from the outside market price, Geneva can trade on the gap. It keeps 35 cents of every dollar of difference, on up to 40,000 barrels a day, and that shows up as Geneva's profit. Here's the key point: the price doesn't change what Halden earns in total. It only changes which part of Halden gets the credit.
4.new_pages_note: New this quarter: what Baton Rouge pays for Texas crude, on your Trading & finance page. It stays there for the rest of the course.

4.marchetti: Oil is at $74 a barrel, and traders expect it to stay about there. What I keep looking at is Europe: refineries there are making only $4.60 on each barrel, and the ones around Rotterdam are slowing down. Honestly, I don't have a call on next quarter's oil price that I'd bet a refinery on.

bands.title: Baton Rouge's best quarter since the merger
paragraphs: Baton Rouge had its best quarter since the merger. Marcus sent the plant a thank-you note and made sure you were copied. Meanwhile, the oil fields' profit dropped to almost nothing on paper, and Ingrid asked Grant why.
Geneva stopped making money on the gap in Halden's own crude prices. Kuhn didn't mention it.

bands.title: Nothing changed, and everyone noticed
paragraphs: You kept the market price the old presidents used. The oil fields had a strong quarter on paper. Baton Rouge's numbers stayed thin, and Marcus sent you an email complaining about it, with the CEO copied.
Geneva had a quiet quarter. Kuhn didn't complain.

bands.title: Geneva had another great quarter
paragraphs: You moved the price, but only partway. The oil fields and Baton Rouge both posted so-so numbers, and neither side was happy.
Geneva made {geneva} on the gap between your price and the outside market. Kuhn sent Grant a short note about it. Grant forwarded it to you without a word.

story.closing: Here's the thing: Halden as a whole made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation, exactly what it would have made at any price. The money just moved from one column to another. Next on Grant's mind: currencies, before the Norwegian krone moves again.

news.title: Lenders are asking about internal prices
news.body: Several companies in your class changed what their refineries pay for their own crude this quarter. Banks have started asking about it when they review loans.

news.title: European refineries slowed down again
news.body: Several refineries around Rotterdam ran below 80% for another quarter. Traders say Europe can make more diesel than it can sell.

cost.why: You set Baton Rouge's crude price at cost. His refinery just had its best quarter since the merger.
The oil fields' profit collapsed on paper, and nobody asked her first.
Geneva can't make money on the price gap anymore.

market.why: You kept the old price after he'd asked you to change it.

between.why: Geneva made money on the gap you left.
He's asked twice why Geneva's profit keeps going up.
